notes.front: What is a “servant-leader”, in the history of the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: The 2017 Scrum Guide’s description of the Scrum Master: a servant-leader for the Scrum Team.
notes.explanation: The revision history shows the phrase in the Scrum Master text as reworded for the 2017 Guide; the 2020 Guide no longer uses it.
notes.example: Like an older edition of a rule book: a study guide from 2017 that calls the Scrum Master a servant-leader uses words the 2020 Guide no longer uses.
notes.source: Scrum Guide Revision History, “Changes between 2016 and 2017 Scrum Guides”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the Scrum Master carry out their accountability for the Scrum Team’s effectiveness?
notes.back: By enabling the Scrum Team to improve its practices, within the Scrum framework.
notes.explanation: Two limits follow from the wording: the team does the improving, and the changes stay inside the Scrum framework.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master is accountable for the Scrum Team’s effectiveness. They do this by enabling the Scrum Team to improve its practices, within the Scrum framework.

notes.front: Scrum Masters are {{c1::true leaders}} who serve the Scrum Team and the larger organization.
notes.explanation: Leadership and service sit in one phrase, and the service reaches past the team to the organisation.
notes.evidence: Scrum Masters are true leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the larger organization.

notes.front: Is the Scrum Guide’s list of ways the Scrum Master serves the Scrum Team a complete list?
notes.back: No. The Guide says the Scrum Master serves the team “in several ways, including” the four it names.
notes.explanation: “Including” leaves room for other forms of service that fit the accountability.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master serves the Scrum Team in several ways, including:

notes.front: What does the Scrum Master help the Scrum Team focus on creating?
notes.back: High-value Increments that meet the Definition of Done.
notes.explanation: Value and quality are joined in one duty: an Increment has to be both high-value and Done.
notes.evidence: Helping the Scrum Team focus on creating high-value Increments that meet the Definition of Done;

notes.front: In the Scrum Guide’s words, what does the Scrum Master do about impediments to the Scrum Team’s progress?
notes.back: Causes their removal.
notes.explanation: The wording is “causing”, not “removing”: the Scrum Master makes sure impediments go, which need not mean doing it all personally.
notes.evidence: Causing the removal of impediments to the Scrum Team’s progress;

notes.front: When does the Scrum Master take part in the Daily Scrum as a Developer?
notes.back: When they are actively working on items in the Sprint Backlog.
notes.explanation: The Daily Scrum is an event for the Developers, so it is the Sprint Backlog work, not the Scrum Master title, that brings them in.
notes.evidence: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers of the Scrum Team. To reduce complexity, it is held at the same time and place every working day of the Sprint. If the Product Owner or Scrum Master are actively working on items in the Sprint Backlog, they participate as Developers.

notes.front: What did the 2017 Scrum Guide say the Scrum Master was responsible for?
notes.back: Promoting and supporting Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide.
notes.explanation: The 2017 text added that Scrum Masters did this by helping everyone understand Scrum theory, practices, rules and values.
notes.source: Scrum Guide Revision History, “Changes between 2016 and 2017 Scrum Guides”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the 2017 wording, what did the Scrum Master help people outside the Scrum Team understand?
notes.back: Which of their interactions with the Scrum Team were helpful and which were not.
notes.explanation: The 2017 text went on to say the Scrum Master helped everyone change those interactions to maximise the value the team created.
notes.source: Scrum Guide Revision History, “Changes between 2016 and 2017 Scrum Guides”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the 2020 Scrum Guide’s description of the Scrum Master differ from the 2017 “servant-leader” wording?
notes.back: 2017: a servant-leader for the Scrum Team. 2020: true leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the larger organisation.
notes.explanation: The 2017 wording is recorded in the Scrum Guide Revision History; service stays at the centre, and the 2020 phrase names the larger organisation alongside the team.
notes.evidence: Scrum Masters are true leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the larger organization.

notes.front: What is the difference between the Scrum Master “causing the removal” of impediments and removing every impediment personally?
notes.back: The Guide asks the Scrum Master to cause removal, which can mean helping others, including the team, remove them.
notes.explanation: The same list asks the Scrum Master to coach team members in self-management, so helping the team clear its own impediments also fits.
notes.evidence: Coaching the team members in self-management and cross-functionality; - Helping the Scrum Team focus on creating high-value Increments that meet the Definition of Done; - Causing the removal of impediments to the Scrum Team’s progress;

notes.front: Does accountability for the Scrum Team’s effectiveness make the Scrum Master the team’s manager?
notes.back: No. The Scrum Master enables the team to improve its practices; they do not decide who does what.
notes.explanation: The Guide says there are no hierarchies within a Scrum Team, and that the team internally decides who does what, when and how.
notes.evidence: Within a Scrum Team, there are no sub-teams or hierarchies. It is a cohesive unit of professionals focused on one objective at a time, the Product Goal. Scrum Teams are cross-functional, meaning the members have all the skills necessary to create value each Sprint. They are also self-managing, meaning they internally decide who does what, when, and how.

notes.front: In an organisation “doing Scrum”, a committee of five business analysts orders the Product Backlog and there is no Product Owner. The committee is happy with this. What does the Scrum Master’s accountability call for?
notes.back: A: help everyone understand Scrum and work toward one Product Owner, establishing Scrum as the Guide defines it.
notes.choices:
A) Helping everyone understand Scrum theory and practice and working toward a single Product Owner, since the Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum as defined in the Guide
B) Accepting the committee as a local adaptation, since everyone is happy
C) Taking the Product Owner accountability in addition to being Scrum Master
D) Reporting the committee to senior management as non-compliant
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Scrum Master establishes Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide, and the Guide says the Product Owner is one person, not a committee. C: this hides the gap instead of helping the organisation understand and fill it. D: the Scrum Master’s route is helping people understand Scrum, not reporting them.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Master’s accountability is to the Guide’s definition of Scrum, pursued by helping people understand it.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide. They do this by helping everyone understand Scrum theory and practice, both within the Scrum Team and the organization.

notes.front: Members of the sales department keep emailing Developers directly with “urgent” feature requests, and the Developers feel obliged to start on them. What is the Scrum Master’s most useful step?
notes.back: C: help sales understand that changes go through the Product Owner, who orders the Product Backlog.
notes.choices:
A) Collect the requests and add them to the Sprint Backlog personally
B) Tell the Developers to ignore all email from sales
C) Help the sales staff understand how Scrum works: those who want the Product Backlog changed try to convince the Product Owner
D) Ask the systems administrators to block email between sales and the Developers
notes.choicesExplained: B: this leaves sales without a way in and teaches them nothing about how Scrum works. A: the Scrum Master would bypass the Product Owner just as sales did. D: a technical block removes contact without helping anyone understand Scrum.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Master establishes Scrum by helping everyone, including the wider organisation, understand Scrum theory and practice.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner is one person, not a committee. The Product Owner may represent the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog. Those wanting to change the Product Backlog can do so by trying to convince the Product Owner.

notes.front: The team’s results have slipped for three Sprints. A manager asks the Scrum Master for a report rating each Developer’s performance. What best fits the Scrum Master’s accountability?
notes.back: B: work with the Scrum Team on improving its practices, and explain this to the manager.
notes.choices:
A) Write the report, since the Scrum Master is accountable for effectiveness
B) Work with the Scrum Team on improving its practices, and help the manager see that effectiveness is pursued by the team, not rated person by person
C) Ask the Product Owner to rate the Developers instead
D) Refuse and tell the manager that performance is none of their business
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide’s route to effectiveness is enabling the team to improve its practices, not rating individuals. D: the Scrum Master serves the organisation too and should help the manager understand, not shut them out. C: the problem is individual rating itself, whoever does it.
notes.explanation: The Guide makes the Scrum Master accountable for the team’s effectiveness and names the method: enabling the team to improve its practices.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master is accountable for the Scrum Team’s effectiveness. They do this by enabling the Scrum Team to improve its practices, within the Scrum framework.

notes.front: The Developers propose dropping the Sprint Review: “The Product Owner sees our work every day anyway.” What should the Scrum Master do?
notes.back: A: keep the Sprint Review and help the team improve it, staying within the Scrum framework.
notes.choices:
A) Help the team improve how it works within the Scrum framework: keep the Sprint Review and look at making it more valuable
B) Merge the Sprint Review into the Sprint Retrospective to save time
C) Agree, because the team is self-managing
D) Hold the Sprint Review only every other Sprint
notes.choicesExplained: C: self-management covers how the team does its work, not removing Scrum’s events. B: the two events have different purposes; merging them drops part of the framework. D: every event is an opportunity to inspect and adapt; skipping it loses that opportunity.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Master enables improvement “within the Scrum framework”, which rules out improving by removing parts of it.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master is accountable for the Scrum Team’s effectiveness. They do this by enabling the Scrum Team to improve its practices, within the Scrum framework.

notes.front: A senior leader tells the Scrum Master: “Focus on your team. Organisational matters are not your concern.” How does this fit the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: D: it does not fit: Scrum Masters serve the Scrum Team and the larger organisation.
notes.choices:
A) It fits: the Scrum Master serves only the Scrum Team
B) It fits: the organisation is the Product Owner’s concern
C) It fits, provided the Scrum Master also leads the team
D) It does not: the Guide describes Scrum Masters as true leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the larger organisation
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide explicitly adds the larger organisation. B: the Guide lists ways the Scrum Master serves the organisation too. C: the Guide’s leadership is service to both the team and the organisation.
notes.explanation: The Guide pairs leadership with service and extends that service beyond the team.
notes.evidence: Scrum Masters are true leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the larger organization.

notes.front: Several Developers come to the Scrum Master each morning asking, “What should I work on next?” What is the best response?
notes.back: A: coach them to decide together, with the Sprint Goal in mind, who does what.
notes.choices:
A) Coach them to decide together, with the Sprint Goal in mind, who takes on what
B) Send them to the Product Owner for their assignments
C) Tell each of them to pick whatever looks interesting
D) Hand out the next items each morning to keep things moving
notes.choicesExplained: D: assigning work takes a decision that belongs to the self-managing team. B: this moves the assigning to someone else instead of building self-management. C: the choice should serve the Sprint Goal, made together, not left to personal preference.
notes.explanation: Coaching team members in self-management is one of the ways the Guide says the Scrum Master serves the Scrum Team.
notes.evidence: Coaching the team members in self-management and cross-functionality;

notes.front: Only one Developer knows how to deploy the product. When she is away, nothing can be released. How can the Scrum Master best help?
notes.back: D: coach the team in cross-functionality so that the skill is shared.
notes.choices:
A) Learn to deploy and do it personally when she is away
B) Ask for a separate deployment team to take over releases
C) Ask her to postpone all leave
D) Coach the team in cross-functionality, so that its members share or acquire the skills they need
notes.choicesExplained: B: this creates a hand-off outside the team instead of building cross-functionality within it. C: this treats the symptom and leaves the team no more cross-functional. A: the Scrum Master would become the new single point of failure.
notes.explanation: The Guide asks the Scrum Master to coach cross-functionality, and says Scrum engages people who share or acquire skills as needed.
notes.evidence: Coaching the team members in self-management and cross-functionality;

notes.front: At each Sprint Review, the Developers present items that are “done apart from testing”. Stakeholders assume the items can be released. What should the Scrum Master help the team focus on?
notes.back: A: Increments that meet the Definition of Done; undone work is not presented.
notes.choices:
A) Creating high-value Increments that meet the Definition of Done, since undone work cannot even be presented at the Sprint Review
B) Presenting the items with a clear caveat about testing
C) Counting the items as half done in the Increment
D) Extending the Sprint until testing is finished
notes.choicesExplained: B: an item that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be presented at the Sprint Review. C: work is either part of the Increment because it meets the Definition of Done, or it is not. D: Sprints are fixed-length; the problem is quality within the Sprint.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Master’s service joins value with quality, and the Guide sends work that is not Done back to the Product Backlog.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”
notes.evidence: If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. Instead, it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.

notes.front: For weeks, the Scrum Team has waited days for another department to provide test environments. The Developers have tried asking and got nowhere. What should the Scrum Master do?
notes.back: C: work with the department and the team to get the barrier removed.
notes.choices:
A) Tell the Developers to wait: it is outside the team’s control
B) Build the environments personally every night
C) Work with the other department and the team to get the barrier removed
D) Suggest skipping testing until environments are available
notes.choicesExplained: B: this may help briefly, but it hides the organisational problem and makes the Scrum Master a bottleneck. A: causing the removal of impediments is part of the Scrum Master’s service to the team. D: quality does not decrease during the Sprint.
notes.explanation: The Guide asks the Scrum Master to cause the removal of impediments, and this one lies outside the team’s reach.
notes.evidence: Causing the removal of impediments to the Scrum Team’s progress;

notes.front: At the Daily Scrum, a Developer says she is blocked by a question about a library’s licence. The company’s legal contact answers such questions within a day, and any Developer can ask. What should the Scrum Master do?
notes.back: A: encourage the Developers to resolve it themselves, stepping in only if needed.
notes.choices:
A) Encourage the Developers to contact legal themselves, and step in only if they cannot resolve it
B) Log it and discuss it at the Sprint Retrospective
C) Take the question to legal personally, as removing impediments is the Scrum Master’s job
D) Tell the Developer to choose a different library without asking
notes.choicesExplained: C: the Guide says “causing the removal”; the team can remove this one itself. B: waiting delays an adjustment that can be made now. D: how to do the work is for the Developers to decide, and the question may have a simple answer.
notes.explanation: Helping the team clear an impediment it can handle itself fits both “causing the removal” and coaching self-management.
notes.evidence: Coaching the team members in self-management and cross-functionality; - Helping the Scrum Team focus on creating high-value Increments that meet the Definition of Done; - Causing the removal of impediments to the Scrum Team’s progress;

notes.front: Sprint Planning for the team’s two-week Sprints regularly runs to nine hours over two days. What is the Scrum Master’s concern here?
notes.back: C: keep the event within its timebox by helping the team find the cause.
notes.choices:
A) Formally extending the timebox, as the team clearly needs more time
B) Splitting Sprint Planning into two separate events
C) Ensuring the event is kept within its timebox, by helping the team find why planning runs so long
D) Having the Scrum Master write the plan in advance to save time
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide sets a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint; timeboxes are maximums. B: this changes the event rather than addressing why it runs long. D: the plan is created by the Scrum Team; the Scrum Master does not write it for them.
notes.explanation: The Guide asks the Scrum Master to ensure events are kept within the timebox, and Sprint Planning’s maximum is eight hours for a one-month Sprint.
notes.evidence: Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint. For shorter Sprints, the event is usually shorter.

notes.front: Sprint Retrospectives have turned into blame sessions, and two Developers now stay silent. What should the Scrum Master do?
notes.back: C: help make the event positive and productive again.
notes.choices:
A) Cancel Retrospectives until relationships improve
B) Invite the line manager to keep order
C) Help the team make the event positive and productive again, for example by changing how it is run
D) Leave it to the team, since it is self-managing
notes.choicesExplained: A: failing to hold an event loses an opportunity to inspect and adapt. B: this adds hierarchy to a team that has none, and may silence people further. D: ensuring events are positive and productive is part of the Scrum Master’s service.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Master ensures that all events are positive and productive, not just that they take place.
notes.evidence: Ensuring that all Scrum events take place and are positive, productive, and kept within the timebox.

notes.front: A department head criticises the Scrum Master for not attending the Daily Scrum. The Developers hold it every day, within 15 minutes, and use it to plan. Is the Scrum Master failing in their accountability?
notes.back: A: no; it is the Developers’ event, and the Scrum Master need not attend.
notes.choices:
A) No: the Daily Scrum is an event for the Developers, and the Scrum Master ensures it happens and works well without having to attend
B) Yes: the Scrum Master must attend to take notes for management
C) Yes: the Scrum Master must run every Daily Scrum
D) No, but only because the Product Owner runs it instead
notes.choicesExplained: C: the Guide gives the Daily Scrum to the Developers and requires no facilitator. B: nothing in the Guide makes the Daily Scrum a reporting event. D: the Product Owner does not run it either; it belongs to the Developers.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Master ensures that events take place and are positive, productive and timeboxed; the Guide does not require them to attend an event that belongs to the Developers.
notes.evidence: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers of the Scrum Team. To reduce complexity, it is held at the same time and place every working day of the Sprint. If the Product Owner or Scrum Master are actively working on items in the Sprint Backlog, they participate as Developers.

notes.front: This Sprint, the Scrum Master is also writing code for two items in the Sprint Backlog. How do they take part in the Daily Scrum?
notes.back: D: as a Developer, because they are working on Sprint Backlog items.
notes.choices:
A) They should not work on Sprint Backlog items at all
B) As an observer only, because they are the Scrum Master
C) As its facilitator, since the Scrum Master always runs it
D) As a Developer, since they are actively working on Sprint Backlog items
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide says a Scrum Master working on Sprint Backlog items participates as a Developer. C: the Guide assigns no facilitator to the Daily Scrum. A: the Guide allows for it, and says how they then take part.
notes.explanation: Participation follows the work: anyone actively working on Sprint Backlog items takes part as a Developer.
notes.evidence: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers of the Scrum Team. To reduce complexity, it is held at the same time and place every working day of the Sprint. If the Product Owner or Scrum Master are actively working on items in the Sprint Backlog, they participate as Developers.

notes.front: An organisation proposes two Scrum Masters for one Scrum Team: one for “technical matters” and one for “business matters”. What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: B: A Scrum Team has one Scrum Master
notes.choices:
A) Two are allowed as long as their duties do not overlap
B) A Scrum Team has one Scrum Master
C) Two are allowed for teams larger than ten people
D) Each Developer may choose which Scrum Master to work with
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide says the Scrum Team consists of one Scrum Master. C: the Guide sets no such exception. D: there is one Scrum Master for the whole team.
notes.explanation: The Guide fixes one Scrum Master and one Product Owner per Scrum Team.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team consists of one Scrum Master, one Product Owner, and Developers.

notes.front: Halfway through a Sprint, a senior manager tells the Scrum Master to cancel it because a new priority has come up. What should the Scrum Master do?
notes.back: D: explain that only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint, and connect the manager with the Product Owner.
notes.choices:
A) Cancel the Sprint, since the request comes from senior management
B) Ask the Developers to vote on cancelling
C) Refuse and tell the manager to wait until the Sprint Review
D) Explain that only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint, and help the manager take the concern to the Product Owner
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide gives the authority to cancel to the Product Owner only. B: the Developers do not hold the authority to cancel either. C: the Product Owner may cancel if the Sprint Goal is obsolete; the manager should be helped to raise it, not blocked.
notes.explanation: A Sprint could be cancelled if its Sprint Goal becomes obsolete, and the Guide puts that decision with the Product Owner alone.
notes.evidence: A Sprint could be cancelled if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel the Sprint.

notes.front: A stakeholder with edit rights has been reordering the Product Backlog at night to move his items up. The Product Owner is unhappy but reluctant to confront him. What is the Scrum Master’s best step?
notes.back: B: help the stakeholder see that changes go through the Product Owner, and support the Product Owner.
notes.choices:
A) Remove the stakeholder’s access without telling anyone
B) Help the stakeholder understand that changes to the Product Backlog go through convincing the Product Owner, and support the Product Owner in that conversation
C) Leave it: the Product Backlog is the Product Owner’s problem
D) Reorder the Product Backlog back personally each morning
notes.choicesExplained: A: this hides the problem without helping anyone understand how Scrum works. C: the Scrum Master serves the Product Owner and helps the organisation understand Scrum. D: the Scrum Master would be managing the Product Backlog, which the Product Owner is accountable for.
notes.explanation: The Guide says those wanting to change the Product Backlog do so by trying to convince the Product Owner.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner is one person, not a committee. The Product Owner may represent the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog. Those wanting to change the Product Backlog can do so by trying to convince the Product Owner.

notes.front: The Product Owner asks the Scrum Master to settle a technical design disagreement among the Developers, “since you understand the architecture best”. What should the Scrum Master do?
notes.back: C: leave the decision with the Developers and coach them to reach it together.
notes.choices:
A) Decide the design, since the Product Owner asked
B) Ask the Product Owner to decide, as they are accountable for value
C) Leave the decision with the Developers, and coach them in reaching it together
D) Put the disagreement to a vote of the whole organisation
notes.choicesExplained: A: no one else tells the Developers how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments. B: the Product Owner is accountable for value, not for how the work is done. D: the decision belongs to the Developers, not to outsiders.
notes.explanation: How the work is done is at the sole discretion of the Developers; the Scrum Master’s part is coaching their self-management.
notes.evidence: How this is done is at the sole discretion of the Developers. No one else tells them how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments of value.

notes.front: Management asks the Scrum Master to write a weekly status report on the team’s progress. The Sprint is two weeks long. What best serves the organisation?
notes.back: D: help management use the empirical approach, such as inspecting the Increment at the Sprint Review.
notes.choices:
A) Write the reports, since serving the organisation means giving it what it asks for
B) Refuse, since Scrum forbids status reports
C) Ask the Developers to write the reports during the Daily Scrum
D) Help management understand and use the empirical approach, such as inspecting the Increment with the team at the Sprint Review
notes.choicesExplained: A: serving the organisation means helping it understand Scrum, not replacing inspection with reports. B: the Guide forbids no such thing; the issue is that reports do not replace empiricism. C: this turns the Developers’ planning event into reporting for others.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Master establishes Scrum by helping everyone, the organisation included, understand Scrum theory and practice.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide. They do this by helping everyone understand Scrum theory and practice, both within the Scrum Team and the organization.

notes.front: A newly formed team of quiet Developers asks the Scrum Master to lead their Daily Scrum “for good”. What is the Scrum Master’s best long-term aim?
notes.back: D: coach the Developers to run their own Daily Scrum.
notes.choices:
A) Lead it permanently, as the team requested
B) Replace it with a written update each morning
C) Ask the Product Owner to lead it instead
D) Coach the Developers to run the Daily Scrum themselves, as it is their event
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Daily Scrum is an event for the Developers, and the Scrum Master coaches self-management. C: this moves leadership of the Developers’ event to someone else. B: the Daily Scrum’s structure is the Developers’ choice, but it remains an event that produces a plan.
notes.explanation: Helping at first can be fine, but the service the Guide names is coaching self-management, and the event belongs to the Developers.
notes.evidence: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers of the Scrum Team. To reduce complexity, it is held at the same time and place every working day of the Sprint. If the Product Owner or Scrum Master are actively working on items in the Sprint Backlog, they participate as Developers.

notes.front: Two days before a release, the Product Owner asks the Scrum Master to agree that the security checks in the Definition of Done can be skipped “just this once”. What should the Scrum Master do?
notes.back: B: explain that undone work is not part of the Increment, and help renegotiate scope instead.
notes.choices:
A) Agree, as the Product Owner is accountable for value
B) Help the Product Owner see that work which does not meet the Definition of Done is not part of the Increment, and explore renegotiating scope instead
C) Agree, if the Developers promise to finish the checks next Sprint
D) Let the Developers vote on skipping the checks
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Product Owner’s accountability does not include lowering the Definition of Done. C: work that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be released now. D: the Developers are required to conform to the Definition of Done, so it is not theirs to vote away.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Master helps the team focus on Increments that meet the Definition of Done, and the Guide keeps undone work out of the Increment.
notes.evidence: Work cannot be considered part of an Increment unless it meets the Definition of Done.

notes.front: The Daily Scrum has grown to 40 minutes as the Developers solve problems in detail during it. What should the Scrum Master help them see?
notes.back: A: keep it to 15 minutes; detailed discussions can happen later in the day.
notes.choices:
A) The Daily Scrum is 15 minutes; detailed discussions can happen afterwards, as Developers often meet throughout the day
B) The timebox can be extended when the problems are important
C) Problem-solving should wait for the Sprint Retrospective
D) The Scrum Master should cut people off after two minutes each
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event. C: the Developers may adjust their plan and discuss details at any time. D: the Developers choose the structure; the Scrum Master helps rather than imposes one.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Master ensures events are kept within the timebox, and the Guide says the Daily Scrum is not the only time Developers adjust their plan.
notes.evidence: The Daily Scrum is not the only time Developers are allowed to adjust their plan. They often meet throughout the day for more detailed discussions about adapting or re-planning the rest of the Sprint’s work.

notes.front: Two Developers have argued about coding standards for three Sprints. The team asks the Scrum Master to “just decide”. What is the best response?
notes.back: C: coach the Developers to resolve it themselves as accountable professionals.
notes.choices:
A) Decide the standard, as the team asked
B) Escalate it to the line manager
C) Coach the Developers to resolve it among themselves, as professionals who hold each other accountable
D) Move one of the Developers to another team
notes.choicesExplained: A: the decision is the self-managing team’s; the Scrum Master coaches rather than rules. B: this adds a hierarchy the Scrum Team does not have. D: this removes a person rather than helping the team manage itself.
notes.explanation: The Guide makes the Developers accountable for holding each other accountable as professionals, and asks the Scrum Master to coach self-management.
notes.evidence: Holding each other accountable as professionals.

notes.front: The personnel department sets the Scrum Master’s yearly objective as “all features delivered by the dates in the plan”. What should the Scrum Master raise?
notes.back: A: their accountability is Scrum and the team’s effectiveness; in complex work, only what has already happened can inform forecasts.
notes.choices:
A) Their accountability is establishing Scrum and the Scrum Team’s effectiveness, and in complex work only what has already happened can inform forecasts
B) Nothing, since the Scrum Master is accountable for delivery dates
C) Ask for the objective to be moved to the Developers
D) Accept, and add overtime to each Sprint to protect the dates
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide makes the Scrum Master accountable for establishing Scrum and for the team’s effectiveness, not for dates. C: the problem is fixed dates for complex work, not who holds the objective. D: this trades sustainable pace for a plan that empiricism does not support.
notes.explanation: The Guide says that in complex environments what will happen is unknown, and forecasting practices do not replace empiricism.
notes.evidence: While proven useful, these do not replace the importance of empiricism. In complex environments, what will happen is unknown. Only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decision making.

notes.front: A department calls its Scrum Master a “project manager” and expects them to assign tasks to Developers and track hours. What should the Scrum Master do first?
notes.back: C: help the department understand the Scrum Master accountability and the Developers’ own planning.
notes.choices:
A) Accept the title and assign tasks, since the name does not matter
B) Assign tasks, but let the Developers swap them if they like
C) Help the department understand the Scrum Master accountability and that the Developers plan their own work in the Sprint Backlog
D) Resign the Scrum Master accountability
notes.choicesExplained: A: assigning tasks takes over the Developers’ accountability for creating the Sprint Backlog plan. B: the plan is still being made by someone other than the Developers. D: the Scrum Master serves the organisation by helping it understand Scrum, not by walking away.
notes.explanation: The Developers are accountable for creating the plan for the Sprint, and the Scrum Master helps the organisation understand Scrum theory and practice.
notes.evidence: However, the Developers are always accountable for: - Creating a plan for the Sprint, the Sprint Backlog;

notes.front: A new Scrum Master’s training notes say: “The Scrum Master is a servant-leader for the Scrum Team,” and so they ignore the wider organisation. What should they know about the current Scrum Guide?
notes.back: B: the 2020 Guide says true leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the larger organisation.
notes.choices:
A) The servant-leader wording is still current, and the team is their only concern
B) The 2020 Guide calls Scrum Masters true leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the larger organisation
C) The 2020 Guide dropped the idea of service altogether
D) The 2020 Guide makes the Scrum Master the organisation’s line manager
notes.choicesExplained: A: servant-leader is the 2017 wording, and even that text had the Scrum Master helping people outside the Scrum Team; the 2020 Guide names the larger organisation. C: service remains: they are true leaders who serve. D: the Guide describes serving the organisation, not managing it.
notes.explanation: Older material still circulates; the 2020 Guide calls Scrum Masters true leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the larger organisation, and no Guide wording lets them ignore the organisation.
notes.evidence: Scrum Masters are true leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the larger organization.

notes.front: A Scrum Master realises the team now brings every small blocker to them, even ones the Developers could clear in minutes. What should change?
notes.back: D: coach the team to clear what it can itself.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: removing every impediment personally is the Scrum Master’s job
B) Stop helping with impediments entirely
C) Ask the Product Owner to handle small blockers instead
D) Coach the team to remove the impediments it can itself, keeping the Scrum Master for those it cannot
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide says “causing the removal”, which does not require doing it all personally. B: causing the removal of impediments is still part of the Scrum Master’s service. C: this moves the dependency to someone else rather than building self-management.
notes.explanation: Coaching self-management and causing the removal of impediments sit in the same list of services to the team.
notes.evidence: Coaching the team members in self-management and cross-functionality; - Helping the Scrum Team focus on creating high-value Increments that meet the Definition of Done; - Causing the removal of impediments to the Scrum Team’s progress;

notes.front: An experienced engineer joins the team from a company that never used Scrum, and keeps asking why the team “wastes time” on Sprint Reviews. What is the Scrum Master’s most direct responsibility here?
notes.back: C: help him understand Scrum theory and practice.
notes.choices:
A) Excusing him from Sprint Reviews until he sees their value
B) Asking the Developers to explain Scrum to him in their spare time
C) Helping him understand Scrum theory and practice, including why the events exist
D) Telling him that Scrum rules are not open to questions
notes.choicesExplained: A: this removes the chance to learn by taking part in the events. B: helping everyone understand Scrum is the Scrum Master’s accountability. D: questions are an opening to help him understand; the Guide describes teaching, not silencing.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Master establishes Scrum by helping everyone understand Scrum theory and practice, new team members included.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide. They do this by helping everyone understand Scrum theory and practice, both within the Scrum Team and the organization.

notes.front: A Developer often misses commitments made to team-mates. The other Developers ask the Scrum Master to “manage him”. What is the best response?
notes.back: A: coach the Developers to hold each other accountable directly.
notes.choices:
A) Coach the Developers to raise it with him directly, as professionals who hold each other accountable
B) Manage him, as the Scrum Master is accountable for effectiveness
C) Report him to the personnel department
D) Ask the Product Owner to give him fewer items
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Scrum Master enables improvement; holding each other accountable is the Developers’ accountability. C: this skips the team’s own accountability and adds a hierarchy. D: this works around the issue rather than helping the team address it.
notes.explanation: The Guide lists holding each other accountable as professionals among the Developers’ own accountabilities.
notes.evidence: Holding each other accountable as professionals.
